accepted.question_text: Does every doubly connected periodic Fatou component of a meromorphic function have to be a Herman ring, rather than some other kind of doubly connected periodic component?
accepted.context_brief: Characterization of doubly connected periodic Fatou components

evidence.quote: Question: Is any doubly connected periodic Fatou component of a meromorphic function always a Herman ring?

Herman ring is a doubly connected periodic Fatou component. However, the opposite has not been proven yet. Is every doubly connected periodic Fatou component of a meromorphic function always a Herman ring?

accepted.question_text: A Siegel disk is guaranteed by the presence of a suitable periodic point, namely a Siegel point. Is there an analogous kind of point or other intrinsic dynamical marker whose existence would guarantee that the map has a Herman ring?

evidence.quote: Siegel discs and Herman rings show quasi-periodic dynamics, but the latter are seen in annular domains. This adds topological complexity and richness to dynamical classifications. Furthermore, a specific kind of periodic point known as a Siegel point guarantees the existence of a Siegel disk. Is there a point whose existence will guarantee the Herman ring’s existence?

accepted.question_text: Which rational maps, especially in low degrees such as 3 and 4, admit Herman rings? More specifically, can one give necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a Herman ring in terms of the map's degree, the configuration of critical orbits, and combinatorial data, and can one describe the associated parameter slices using tools such as Teichmuller theory and quasiconformal deformation theory?
accepted.context_brief: Classification of rational maps with Herman rings

evidence.quote: It is known that rational functions of degree 2 cannot have any Herman rings. However, further investigation is needed to classify all rational functions that can admit Herman rings, particularly in low degrees (degree 3 or 4), where examples are still limited. Despite several known constructions, a complete characterization of rational maps admitting Herman rings is still lacking. In particular, it remains open to identify necessary and sufficient conditions in terms of degree, critical orbit configurations, and combinatorial data. It is also fascinating to investigate parameter slices for families of functions with a Herman ring. Using Teichmuller theory and quasiconformal deformation theory to map out these regions can also be explored.

accepted.question_text: How are Herman rings created or destroyed when a rational or transcendental map is perturbed, and what is the structure and size of the parameter sets in natural families for which Herman rings occur?

evidence.quote: The behavior of Herman rings under perturbations of the underlying map is not well understood. In particular, the mechanisms by which Herman rings are created or destroyed in parameter space remain to be clarified. Also, the structure and size of the set of parameters corresponding to maps with Herman rings in natural families of rational and transcendental maps are still largely unknown.

accepted.question_text: What geometric regularity can the boundary components of a Herman ring have? In particular, under what hypotheses are these boundaries Jordan curves or quasicircles, when can they have fractal structure, what can be said about their Hausdorff dimension or Lebesgue measure, and can a Herman-ring boundary ever have positive area?

evidence.quote: The geometric nature of the boundary components of Herman rings is largely mysterious. In particular, it is not known under what conditions these boundaries are Jordan curves, quasicircles, or have fractal structure. Little is known about the Hausdorff dimension or Lebesgue measure of the boundary of a Herman ring. Whether such boundaries can have positive area is an open question.

accepted.question_text: Can one develop an obstruction theory and identify structural conditions under which a transcendental map with a Herman ring can be conformally mated with the action of a Fuchsian group or a subgroup of PSL(2, Z) on the upper half-plane? More specifically, when can a topological mating between the map and the group action be defined, when can that topological mating be promoted to a conformal one, and what dynamical feature distinguishes the resulting correspondence map when the function has a Herman ring?
accepted.context_brief: Conformal matings in the transcendental setting

evidence.quote: A conformal mating is a construction that "glues" the Julia set of a function to the action of a Fuchsian group (or subgroup of PSL(2, Z)) on the upper half-plane, creating a single function that incorporates both behaviors consistently-conformally and dynamically.

Conformal mating in the transcendental setting is far less developed than in the polynomial or rational case. Hence, one can study to develop an obstruction theory and identify structural conditions under which such matings could theoretically exist. The goal should be to determine when a topological mating between the map with a Herman ring and the group action can be defined, and whether such a topological mating can be promoted to a conformal one. What distinguishes the correspondence map whenever the function has a Herman ring?

accepted.question_text: Must every rational map that has a Herman ring also have buried Julia components, or are additional global dynamical or topological assumptions needed before the existence of a Herman ring forces buried Julia components to appear?

evidence.quote: The presence of a Herman ring strongly suggests, but does not automatically guarantee, the existence of buried Julia components. In many known constructions, rational maps with Herman rings do exhibit buried Julia components arising from this topological separation. However, the existence of buried Julia components depends on the global arrangement of Fatou components and how the Julia set accumulates on their boundaries. It remains a subtle problem to determine whether every rational map with a Herman ring must contain buried Julia components or whether additional dynamical or topological conditions are required. As such, the question of whether Herman rings ensure the presence of buried Julia components is an important and largely open direction of investigation.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a root-finding method, for instance among generalizations of Newton, Konig, or Chebyshev type methods, whose Fatou set contains a Herman ring?

evidence.quote: To our knowledge, no root-finding method is known to possess a Herman ring in the Fatou set. The same is also true whenever f is an entire function.
Certain root-finding techniques are known to have disconnected Julia sets. This raises the question of whether there is a root-finding method whose Fatou set contains a Herman ring.

accepted.question_text: Given a periodic Herman ring H of period p for a meromorphic function, can one prove an upper bound on p in terms of the number h of H-relevant poles, complementing the known lower bounds? This is especially asked for meromorphic maps with finitely many poles and at least one omitted value, such as functions of the form E(z)/((z-z0)(z-z1)...(z-zp)) where E is an entire function omitting a finite point.
accepted.context_brief: Upper bounds on period from relevant poles

evidence.quote: Theorem 5.9. Let H be a p-periodic Herman ring of a function f, and let h be the number of H-relevant poles. Then p >= h(h+1)/2.

For a given Herman ring H, Theorem 5.9 provides a lower bound on the period of H in terms of the number of H-relevant poles. Is it possible to find an upper bound on the period of H? This question seems to be more relevant for meromorphic maps with finitely many poles and with an omitted value. Such a function is of the form f(z) = E(z)/((z-z0)(z-z1)...(z-zp)), p > 1 and z0, z1, . . . , zp in C where E is an entire function omitting a finite point.

accepted.question_text: For a meromorphic function with a stable Baker omitted value, can there be infinitely many Herman rings whose periods vary, even though for each fixed period p >= 3 the number of p-periodic Herman rings is known to be finite? In particular, can this happen when the Baker omitted value is the only accumulation point of the critical values?
accepted.context_brief: Infinitely many periods with stable bov

evidence.quote: Theorem 5.11. Let f be a function with a stable bov and p >= 3. Then the number of p-periodic Herman rings is finite.

For a function with a stable bov and fixed p >= 3, Theorem 5.11 proves that the number of p-periodic Herman rings is finite. However, this result does not exclude the possibility of the function having infinitely many Herman rings of different periods. Whether such a situation can occur, particularly when the bov is the only accumulation point of the critical values, remains an open question.

accepted.question_text: For each natural number n, is there a finite upper bound on the number of distinct geometric or combinatorial configurations that an n-cycle of Herman rings of period n can realize?

evidence.quote: Regarding possible configurations of Herman rings, we have the following question: Question: Is there any bound on the possible number of configurations of an n-cycle of Herman rings of period n in N?

accepted.question_text: If a meromorphic function with an omitted value has a quasi-nested wandering domain, must that function necessarily have no Herman rings?

evidence.quote: Chakraborty et al. [10] in 2022 proved that the existence of a quasi-nested wandering domain of a meromorphic function f with an omitted value ensures that there exists no unbounded Fatou component of f giving that an unbounded Herman ring does not exist for f. We make the following conjecture. Conjecture: Meromorphic functions with quasi-nested wandering domains have no Herman rings.

accepted.question_text: If a general transcendental meromorphic function has a finite omitted value, does that condition alone force the map to have no Herman rings of any period?
accepted.context_brief: Finite omitted values obstructing Herman rings

evidence.quote: We propose the following conjecture. Conjecture: If a general meromorphic function has a finite omitted value, it does not have a Herman ring of any period.

However, no known example exists of a function that omits a value and possesses a Herman ring. This has led to the conjecture that a meromorphic function with an omitted value cannot have a Herman ring.
